subject: Economy
theme: Central bank monetary policy and inflation control mechanisms
question_short_text: Post-pandemic rate hikes and CB inflation control assumptions
text:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I:
In the post-pandemic recent past, many Central Banks worldwide had carried out interest rate hikes.

Statement-II:
Central Banks generally assume that they have the ability to counteract the rising consumer prices via monetary policy means.

Which of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
options: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I.
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is not the correct explanation for Statement-I.
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect.
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct.
answerText: (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II is the correct explanation for Statement-I.
explanation: Statement-I is factually correct: the Fed, ECB, BoE, and other major central banks conducted coordinated, aggressive interest rate hikes starting in 2022-2023 to combat post-pandemic inflation. Statement-II is also correct: central banks operate on the assumption that monetary policy tools (primarily interest rates) can control inflation by managing aggregate demand. Statement-II logically explains Statement-I because the rate hikes were undertaken precisely because central banks assume they can counter rising prices through monetary tightening.

research.summary:
This question tests understanding of the causal link between central bank credibility assumptions and actual policy implementation during the post-pandemic inflation surge. Between March 2022 and July 2023, the Fed raised rates 11 times, bringing the federal funds rate from near-zero to 5.25–5.50%; the ECB raised rates by 4.5 percentage points beginning July 2022; and the Bank of England, Bank of Canada, and other major central banks executed similar tightening cycles with unusual synchronicity. This global rate-hike campaign was justified by a core assumption: that central banks possess reliable monetary policy transmission mechanisms to dampen inflation by raising borrowing costs, slowing spending, and reducing aggregate demand.

However, the relationship between the two statements is causal, not merely coincidental. Central banks assumed they could engineer a soft landing—controlling inflation without triggering deep recession—by raising rates. The fact that they executed massive hikes rests on this foundational assumption of policy efficacy. If central banks doubted their ability to influence prices through monetary means, they would not have pursued such aggressive tightening. Statement-II therefore provides the underlying rationale (the theoretical confidence) that motivates the empirical fact (the actual hikes) described in Statement-I.

A subtle trap in this question is thinking that because both statements are true, they might be unrelated. But UPSC is testing whether the student understands that policy action flows from theoretical assumptions. Another potential confusion: students might conflate central bank 'ability' with guaranteed success. Central banks assume they have the power to influence inflation, but outcomes depend on numerous factors (supply shocks, wage dynamics, fiscal policy coordination). The statement does not claim they always succeed, only that they assume the mechanism exists and is operable.
facts: The Fed's 2022-2023 rate hike cycle (11 hikes from March 2022 to July 2023) was the fastest major tightening since the 1980s Volcker era, undertaken to combat inflation that had reached 9.1% in June 2022.
Global central banks raised rates with unprecedented synchronicity in 2022-2023; between September and November 2022 alone, central banks worldwide raised rates by a total of 68%.

Interest rate transmission to inflation typically involves a lag of 12-18 months, meaning central banks operate with significant uncertainty about whether their current decisions will achieve desired inflation outcomes.

Core inflation and energy-driven inflation have different sensitivities to monetary policy; supply shocks (Ukraine war, supply-chain disruptions) limit the effectiveness of demand-side monetary tools alone.

By late 2023, major central banks began pausing rate hikes as inflation moderated, signaling completion of the hike cycle and shifting focus toward assessing whether the assumed policy transmission had succeeded.

sources.title: The Fed's rate hikes timeline and causes (TheStreet)
sources.whyUsed: Verified timeline and magnitude of Fed rate hikes (11 hikes from March 2022 to July 2023) and confirmation that the purpose was to combat post-pandemic inflation.

sources.title: Interest rates are rising globally (World Economic Forum)
sources.whyUsed: Confirmed that central banks worldwide simultaneously raised rates and that they assume interest rates are a primary tool to control inflation.

sources.title: Global Recession Risk and Simultaneous Rate Hikes (World Bank)
sources.whyUsed: Documented the unusual synchronicity of global central bank rate hikes in 2022-2023 (68% increase in rates globally from Sept-Nov 2022) and validated that this was a coordinated response to inflation.

sources.title: Central Banks Hike Interest Rates in Sync to Tame Inflation (IMF)
sources.whyUsed: Explained the theoretical basis: central banks use rate hikes to slow demand and address demand-related inflationary pressures, validating Statement-II's assumption.

sources.title: Global Trend of Central Banks Lowering Interest Rates (OANDA)
sources.whyUsed: Provided broader context on why rate hikes were employed: the mechanism is that higher interest rates make borrowing expensive, slow spending and demand, and dampen inflation.
